card.title: Sixty-Five Squatter Families Moved into Flats at Salem, and Land Taken in Chennai
card.place: Salem city, Tamil Nadu, with land acquisition under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-47980 for the Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780). US$300 million approved 5 July 2005 and effective 19 October 2005; US$290.87 million disbursed. Original closing 30 March 2011; actual closing 31 March 2014. The project was restructured twice: the completion report's text dates the restructurings to August 2009 and January 2012, while its own data sheet dates them to 1 July 2009 and 7 February 2012. It financed 110 sub-projects under the urban investment component as well as the Chennai urban transport sub-component, and paid rehabilitation and resettlement costs: under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, the completion report's cost table gives INR 137.22 million as the revised allocation for rehabilitation and resettlement together with shifting of utilities, against INR 191.21 million spent to March 2014 (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014; IEG ICR Review ICRR14687, 12 May 2015).

card.community: Under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders were affected, including the resettlement of five displaced families. The cost of private land acquisition and resettlement and rehabilitation assistance there was INR 132.32 million, about US$2.20 million, or 8.5 per cent of that sub-component's cost. Under the urban investment component, 110 sub-projects were carried out; private land acquisition was involved in only seven of them and resettlement in one. In all, 21 hectares of private land were acquired from 31 landowners, and about 45 hectares of government land were transferred, including 23 acres of temple land. The resettlement took place in Salem, where 65 squatter families were moved into multi-storied apartments. Total compensation and resettlement assistance for those eight sub-projects came to INR 30 million, 0.73 per cent of their cost. The completion report records instances of delays in paying compensation and resettlement assistance, later addressed after follow-up by the Bank team and the state's urban development fund. At loan closure all compensation and assistance had been paid, except that the 65 families moved into the Salem apartment had not been given title to their flats: under Tamil Nadu rules titles were to be issued in December 2014, at the end of a five-year stay. An end-term impact evaluation of the Salem families found their incomes up, because more family members were working, and their housing better, having moved from huts to built flats. The same evaluation recorded what was wrong: drinking water supply was erratic and flats on the upper floors got no water because of problems lifting it; allotment of flats took no account of the elderly, old and sick, some of whom were put on higher floors; and residents reported thefts and a lack of security. The families kept ties to where they had lived, still sending children to schools there, visiting doctors there and mostly still working there. A separate evaluation of the Chennai transport families found 75 per cent satisfied with the rate of compensation, which the report attributes to a consent award process for private land and payment for structures without depreciation; compensation money was mostly spent on improving houses, 40 per cent of it. Land availability was a running problem: about 16 of the more than 40 sites needed for urban sub-projects had to be changed, for reasons including objections from nearby residents and court cases over unclear land titles.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 3,300 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The Bank's completion report counts 65 squatter families resettled at Salem and five displaced families resettled under the Chennai urban transport sub-component, 70 families in all, alongside 212 title holders and 337 non-title holders affected in Chennai and 31 landowners whose land was acquired.
card.outcome: The loan closed on 31 March 2014 with the 65 Salem families living in the flats but without title to them, which was due in December 2014. The Bank advised Salem Corporation to act on the impact evaluation's findings and to issue the titles when due. No document found records whether the titles were issued.
card.confidence_note: The counts of families, landowners, hectares and the rupee amounts all come from the Bank's own completion report, which also carries the impact evaluation's findings on water, floor allotment and theft at the Salem flats. The Independent Evaluation Group reviewed that report rather than going into the field, so the lender is the only source. The impact evaluation is summarised in the completion report rather than published with it, so its sample size and method are not known, and no independent study of the Salem resettlement was found. The report does not say where in Salem the families were moved from or to.

sources.title: World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, India Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780), ICR00003125
Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, Third Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project (P083780), ICRR14687

card.whole: By the Bank's own count the sub-projects commissioned under the loan brought improved water and sewerage services to more than 2.3 million people, including 440,000 in low-income neighbourhoods. The completion report's results table gives 290,000 new household sewer connections against a target of 150,000, while its annexes give 298,688 for the same item. Tamil Nadu raised US$52 million for urban infrastructure from bonds, public-private deals and household contributions, against a target of US$40 million. The weighted average rate of return across the sub-projects was 19 per cent, highest for water supply at 24 per cent and lowest for roads at 15 per cent. The completion report of 30 September 2014 rates the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 May 2015 rates it Moderately Satisfactory and rates efficiency modest. All the figures are the lender's own and no independent check was found.
card.conditions: Because the money was lent on to many separate sub-projects, the safeguard policies were applied through an Environmental and Social Framework rather than fixed in advance: the framework's screening tools decided, sub-project by sub-project, which policies applied and what plan was needed. The framework was in place by appraisal, was formally approved by a Government of Tamil Nadu order, and was treated as meeting the requirements of the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, OP 4.12. At appraisal the project was recorded as triggering environmental assessment, cultural property and involuntary resettlement (Project Appraisal Document, 25 May 2005). For the Chennai transport works, consultants prepared the environmental management plan and resettlement action plan, the state financing company reviewed and approved them, and the Bank then had to issue a no-objection before the works could be put out to bid; a works contract could be signed only once the land was clear and the resettlement plan had been fully carried out. The implementing agencies were Tamil Nadu Urban Infrastructure Financial Services and, for the transport works, the Chennai Metropolitan Development Authority, and two environmental and social audits were carried out during implementation (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 30 September 2014).

card.title: Market Traders Moved at Kasumbalesa Border Post
card.place: Kasumbalesa border post, Chililabombwe District, Copperbelt Province, Zambia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P071985), SDR 33.5 million (US$50 million equivalent) approved 9 March 2004, with a first additional financing of SDR 16.8 million (US$25 million) and a second of SDR 9.9 million (US$15 million); the completion report's cover gives the credit numbers as IDA-38660, IDA-38661 and IDPA-48210. SDR 59.98 million was disbursed. The project closed on 30 June 2014, seven years after its first closing date. The credit paid for the rehabilitation of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road and for its engineering supervision; the completion report gives the length rehabilitated as 39 km in its results annex and as 40.5 km in its outputs annex, and the Evaluation Group's review gives the road as 40 km. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the implementing agencies' performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (27 April 2015); the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Chililabombwe Municipal Council
companies.role: Its Engineering Section moved the traders, found the new sites and valued what they lost
companies.desc: The local authority for Chililabombwe district in Zambia's Copperbelt Province, about 20 km from the Kasumbalesa border post.

companies.name: Road Development Agency
companies.role: Implementing agency for the road works and the channel through which the compensation receipts were to be passed to the lender
companies.desc: Zambian state road agency, set up in 2005 under this project together with the National Road Fund Agency and the Road Transport and Safety Agency, responsible for the trunk road network.

card.community: In December 2005 traders were moved from the north-eastern side of the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road to the western side, to clear space for trucks waiting to be cleared by immigration at the border. The Environmental Management Unit of the Roads Department, which was responsible for applying the lender's resettlement rules, was told only after the move had happened. The abbreviated resettlement plan written afterwards, in May 2006, states that "because of lack of information and sensitization, the provisions outlined in the Resettlement Policy Framework completed during project preparation have not been followed", and that the plan was written to correct that. The plan lists 67 numbered traders by name and national registration number, some names appearing more than once, and puts the number of people at roughly 65: 23 restaurants, 20 grocery stalls, 21 sellers of vegetables, fruit and other goods, one carpentry business and two pay phones. The sums set were 2,590,000 kwacha for each restaurant, 1,390,000 for each grocery, 400,000 for each market seller, 250,000 for the carpentry and 8,000,000 for each pay phone, 113,410,000 kwacha in all. The costs counted were taking down and rebuilding structures, buying materials, business lost during the move, and transport of materials from Chililabombwe 20 km away. The plan says the host community was the same community, because the move was within the same area, and that the facilities used before the move still served the people who were resettled. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says the government's counterpart funding "was not paid on schedule, only six percent of the required commitments per year, causing delays in implementing the Resettlement Action Plan (RAP), and thus negatively impacting the overall project implementation timetable and costs". The same passage adds that the counterpart funding "was fully realized (US$64.3 million) at project closure as per commitment", and the review rates government performance Moderately Satisfactory.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 67 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The abbreviated resettlement plan's compensation table has 67 numbered entries, with three names repeating, and the plan's own text puts "the total number of people involved" at "roughly sixty-five (65)". That figure is approximate and is attached to the people being compensated; the plan's relocation sentence counts nobody, saying only that "some marketeers had been resettled". No figure in any document for this project carries a relocation verb, so none is counted here.
card.outcome: The plan set out that the contractor would pay each trader in front of a council officer and an officer of the Environmental Management Unit, that each would sign a receipt, and that the signed receipts would go to the Resident Engineer as part of the contractor's monthly claim and on to the Road Development Agency, the National Road Fund Agency and the World Bank. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review of it says whether the money was paid. The completion report's table of safeguard documents records the abbreviated plan as disclosed in July 2006. The road was rehabilitated; the Evaluation Group's review says that at closing several sections, among them Chingola-Kasumbalesa, were in poor condition and in further need of repair.
card.confidence_note: The traders' names, trades and payment amounts come from the borrower's own resettlement plan, published by the World Bank. No independent report of the move was found. The plan was written six months after the move and sets out money still to be paid; no later document states that it was paid.

sources.title: Zambia - Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project: resettlement action plan (Vol. 2 of 2): Abbreviated Resettlement Action Plan - Kasumbalesa Border Post

ICR Review: Zambia - Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (ICRR14779)

Financing Agreement, Credit 3866-1-ZM (Conformed), Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project Additional Financing
Implementation Completion and Results Report, Road Rehabilitation and Maintenance Project (P071985)

card.whole: The credit rehabilitated the Chingola-Kasumbalesa road, given as 39 km in the completion report's results annex, 40.5 km in its outputs annex and 40 km in the Evaluation Group's review, and SDR 59.98 million was spent. Across the whole project, routine maintenance covered 50 per cent of the main road network by June 2014, up from 19.5 per cent in 2004 and two years after the target date, and 505,000 rural people gained all-weather river crossings as all 103 small and medium crossings were completed. The report gives the domestic share of the road budget two ways: 66 per cent in its indicator table, and 55 per cent in 2014 against an unmet target of 66 per cent in its own text. A system for recording road crashes, due by December 2005, was built in 2014 but was not working at closing; the figures come from the lender and the borrower's roads agencies, with no independent check found.
card.conditions: The Bank's completion report records one requirement of the original credit agreement for this project: the National Road Fund Agency prepared a plan for its operations after the project "as required under Section 3.3 of the Development Credit Agreement" (World Bank, Implementation Completion and Results Report, 27 April 2015, paragraph 68). The resettlement policy framework for the project was disclosed in October 2003 and the abbreviated resettlement plan for the Kasumbalesa border post in July 2006, both before the only loan agreement the Bank publishes for this project: the additional financing agreement of 12 April 2007, which required that, before civil works involving resettlement or land taking, Zambia "prepare and implement appropriate resettlement plans for compensation, resettlement and rehabilitation of Displaced Persons, in accordance with the Resettlement Policy Framework" (Financing Agreement, Credit 3866-1 ZA, Schedule 4, Section I.B.2). That agreement postdates the move of the market traders, so it is not carried here as a term that governed it.
card.ct_note: The credit agreement that paid for the border post works, signed in 2004, has not been published. The Bank's document record for the project holds 34 documents, among them the 2004 appraisal document, the completion report and the 2007 additional financing agreement, but not the original development credit agreement for Credit 3866-ZA, and the Bank's document system holds nothing under that credit number. What that agreement required is known only from the single section the completion report cites.

card.title: Uganda's rural electrification credit: lines built before the people under them were paid
card.place: Rural grid extension lines across Uganda, with a focus on the north; point at Kampala

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-45540 and IDA-52340 for the Energy for Rural Transformation Project APL-2 (P112334), a credit of SDR 57.6 million (US$87 million equivalent). Approved 6 April 2009, effective 25 November 2009, closing extended from 30 June 2013 to 30 June 2016, with restructurings on 23 May 2014 and 13 February 2015. Original commitment SDR 49.50 million plus SDR 8.10 million, against SDR 54.51 million disbursed. The project was environmental category B. The implementing agencies included the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Development and the Rural Electrification Agency. The outcome was rated Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory (World Bank Implementation Completion and Results Report, 23 June 2017).

lenders.name: Global Environment Facility
lenders.role: Grant TF-94484 of US$9 million, of which US$7.26 million was disbursed (World Bank completion report).

lenders.name: Global Partnership on Output-Based Aid
lenders.role: Grant TF-10096 of US$5.5 million, of which US$5.49 million was disbursed (World Bank completion report).

card.community: The project extended the rural electricity grid, building 12 distribution lines of almost 1,300 km, and took land and wayleaves for them. The Bank's completion report says the overall safeguards rating 'remained Satisfactory until May 2014 when the rating was downgraded to Moderately Unsatisfactory due to delayed payment of compensations to Project Affected Persons (PAPs) even after most of the grid extension lines and expansion projects had been completed. This was non-compliant with World Bank OP 4.12, which required complete compensations to PAPs prior to the commencement of any civil works.' It says the delays were put down to the directive requiring payment through bank accounts, which most affected people in rural areas did not have. On three further grid extension lines financed at the February 2015 restructuring, it says, 'construction works had finalized well before compensation to PAPs was completed'. The resettlement plan's closure report records that cash payments were finished in December 2016, six months after the project closed, with nearly 90 per cent of affected people paid, rising to over 96 per cent by 1 June 2017, and that an escrow account was opened to hold the money for those still unpaid. The report also records recurring differences between the people identified in the resettlement plans and those identified in the detailed engineering designs, which it says caused contention and conflict among affected people and local leaders. The Bank's own account of its borrower's performance says 'the GoU violated the World Bank OP 4.12 when commenced and even finalized construction of grid extension lines before completing compensation payments to PAPs', and that the money for those payments was not transferred to the Rural Electrification Agency in time. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 14 November 2017 says the agency 'was in noncompliance with the Bank's policy by allowing the start of the construction works before the completion of compensation payments' and that, while the government was late releasing the funds, the agency was also slow to pay when funds were available. No document found gives the number of people affected, counts anyone relocated or names a line or a community.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 12,239 for this project. No Bank document found gives any count of people affected, compensated or relocated, so no figure is entered here. The documents do not explain how ICIJ's figure was arrived at.
card.outcome: The Bank rated the project's outcome Moderately Satisfactory and its own performance Moderately Unsatisfactory, and the Independent Evaluation Group records that weak Bank supervision on the resettlement policy resulted in non-compliance. Compensation payments were still being made a year after the project closed. The Independent Evaluation Group also records that some staff of the Rural Electrification Agency were found to have been involved in fraud and corruption over the verification of solar equipment installations.
card.confidence_note: The breach of the Bank's resettlement policy is stated in the World Bank's own completion report and in the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, which are the only sources found and are the lender reporting on its own project; a search for independent reporting, litigation or a complaint on this project found none. Neither document gives the number of people whose land or wayleaves were taken, names any of the 12 lines or names a community, so the harm recorded here is that compensation was paid late or not at all, without a count of the people it was owed to.

sources.title: Uganda - Energy for Rural Transformation Project APL-2: Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR00004053)
Uganda - UG-Energy for Rural Transformation II: ICR Review

card.whole: By the Bank's own count the project connected 97,753 households against an original target of 109,000 and a revised target of 120,000, and gave 643,674 people access to electricity against a target of 720,000. It electrified 522 health centres against a target of 464, 546 rural schools against 560, and 44 water supply schemes, up from 15; households using solar panels rose from 12,000 to 23,000 against a target of 32,000, and no connections at all were made through independent small grids, against a target of 5,300. The share of the rural population with electricity in the project areas rose from 4 to 7 per cent; the Independent Evaluation Group says the 7 per cent target was itself set from a Uganda Bureau of Statistics survey and that the rise in rural electrification cannot be fully attributed to the project. A second objective, increasing access to information and communication technology in rural Uganda, drew no activity at all, which the Evaluation Group rated Negligible. An economic rate of return of 12 per cent was calculated only at closing, for two of the project's three components, counting avoided diesel and kerosene costs, avoided peak load demand and energy savings. The Evaluation Group rated the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory where the completion report rated it Moderately Satisfactory, and rated efficiency Modest where the completion report rated it Substantial. The figures are the lender's own; no independent check of them was found.
card.conditions: The project triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy because its works took land or limited access to land, along with policies on forests, dam safety and international waterways. A resettlement policy framework and an environmental and social management framework were prepared at appraisal. The resettlement policy required that compensation be paid in full before any civil works began. A government directive required that compensation be paid only through formal bank accounts.

card.title: Two-Year Gap Between Acquisition and Compensation Notices on the Gujarat Highways
card.place: Eight state highway widening and strengthening corridors in Gujarat, which the documents do not name individually, India

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-83130 for the Second Gujarat State Highway Project (P114827). US$175 million approved 13 December 2013, loan agreement dated 12 February 2014, and the full loan amount disbursed. Original closing 31 January 2019, extended by 23 months in the restructuring of 13 September 2018; the project closed 31 December 2020. The borrower's contribution was US$158.50 million and the private sector's US$37.40 million. Component A, Highway Improvement, financed the road works and, within both of its sub-components, support for land acquisition and resettlement, utility relocation, environmental management and supervision. The appraisal document states that all land acquisition and resettlement costs paid in cash were to be met from Government of Gujarat funds, with Bank money covering the consultancies, goods and works for carrying out the resettlement plans. Classified Category A and triggered the Bank's policies on environmental assessment, involuntary resettlement, indigenous peoples, forests and physical cultural resources (IEG ICR Review ICRR0022895, 13 June 2022; World Bank Project Appraisal Document, 7 November 2013).

card.community: The project widened and strengthened eight road corridors and rehabilitated three more added at the September 2018 restructuring: 60.4 km from Radhanpur to Chanasma, 66.8 km from Mehsana to Palanpur including a 5 km bypass at Mehsana, and 27 km from Vallabhipur to Ranghola. At appraisal the social impact assessments expected impacts on about 730 project-affected households, title holders and non-title holders together, 23 hectares of private land, 7 hectares of government land and 304 privately owned structures, mostly shops, from the widening and strengthening works. Three of the corridors passed through Schedule V areas with tribal populations, and the appraisal document recorded three Scheduled Tribe households as affected. In the event, 14.4 hectares of land were acquired during implementation, of which 11.51 hectares were private. Acquisition in the eight corridors took two years. The notification of acquisition was issued in January 2017 under local law, but the notification awarding compensation could only be issued in February 2019, two years later. The Independent Evaluation Group records that the completion report reports no issues with compliance with the involuntary resettlement policy, and that the lengthy land acquisition process delayed implementation and hurt the project's efficiency. District-level grievance redressal committees were set up to take complaints about resettlement and compensation, alongside postal correspondence and approaches to the executive engineers on site. Some religious structures affected by the works were relocated with the cooperation of local communities.
card.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 4,000 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The only count of people in the documents opened is the appraisal estimate of about 730 project-affected households in the Project Appraisal Document, repeated in the ICR Review. No Bank document found gives a count of people relocated.
card.outcome: The loan closed on 31 December 2020 with the full US$175 million disbursed. No Implementation Completion and Results Report for this project is disclosed in the Bank's document archive; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of it, dated 13 June 2022, is the latest public account found.
card.confidence_note: The hectares acquired, the acquisition and compensation notification dates and the appraisal counts come from the Independent Evaluation Group's review and the appraisal document. The completion report itself is not disclosed in the Bank's document archive for this project: a search of all 118 documents listed for P114827, and two separate title searches, return only the Independent Evaluation Group's review. The account here therefore rests on that review's summary of a report the public cannot read, and the lender is the only source. This is the thinnest of the entries kept from this batch: the harm on the record is 11.51 hectares of private land acquired and a two-year gap between the two statutory notices. No document opened says how many households that land came from, how many were paid, what they were paid, whether anyone was left out, or when money reached people, and the Independent Evaluation Group records that the completion report reported no compliance issues with the involuntary resettlement policy.

sources.title: Independent Evaluation Group, ICR Review, Second Gujarat State Highway Project (P114827)
World Bank, Project Appraisal Document, India Second Gujarat State Highway Project (P114827)

card.whole: The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 13 June 2022 records 423 km of state highway built, against a target of 460.7 km, and 292.80 km rehabilitated as targeted, 715.80 km in all. Car journey times on project roads fell from 75 to 57 minutes per 50 km, against a target of 50 minutes, and truck journeys from 85 to 67 minutes against a target of 65; average road surface roughness was 1,758 mm per km, inside the 2,000 mm standard. The share of all classified state roads in good or fair condition rose from 43 per cent to 81 per cent against a revised target of 75 per cent, but the review states that this indicator counted roads the project did not pay for, and puts the project-financed roads' own share of the rise at 11.1 percentage points against a revised target of 12. The rate of return calculated after closing was 51.9 per cent against 35.1 per cent at appraisal, which the review attributes to lower construction contract costs and to some roads finishing early; the net present value after closing was Rs 20.2 billion against Rs 21.3 billion at appraisal, which the review attributes to traffic volumes below forecast during the COVID-19 slowdown. The review rates efficiency Substantial and the outcome Moderately Satisfactory. The completion report itself is not disclosed, so these figures exist only as the review's summary of it, and no independent check was found.
card.conditions: The project was classified category A and triggered five safeguard policies: environmental assessment, forests, physical cultural resources, indigenous peoples and involuntary resettlement. Resettlement action plans were prepared for the eight widening corridors and an Indigenous People's Development Plan for the corridors through Schedule V tribal areas, with free, prior and informed consultation held there; drafts of the resettlement policy framework, the action plans and the development plans were published by the state Roads and Buildings Department and by the Bank. The framework set compensation for land at market value and structures at replacement cost, provided shifting and transitional allowances and income generation assistance, extended replacement cost and time to remove assets to people without title, and required the amounts to be updated every year. All land acquisition and resettlement costs paid in cash were to come from Government of Gujarat funds, with loan money paying only for the consultancies, goods and works needed to carry the plans out. Loan covenants required Gujarat to obtain every necessary permit and clearance before civil works started on any road, to report quarterly on safeguard compliance, and to maintain a district-level grievance redress mechanism for resettlement and rehabilitation (Project Appraisal Document, 7 November 2013).

card.title: Zambia 2004 wage freeze and unhired teachers

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a wage cap with the government in 2003 after an unbudgeted pay rise and housing allowance; HIPC debt relief depended on meeting programme benchmarks (IRIN 2005; IMF letter 2004).

card.community: Oxfam counted a shortage of about 9,000 teachers while around 12,000 trained teachers could not be put on the payroll because of a spending ceiling (IRIN 2004). The teachers' union said some rural pupils saw no teacher during 2004. An income tax rise of up to 40% hit about 495,000 workers (IRIN 2005).
card.outcome: Workers struck against the tax rise and wage cap; the ZCTU said 90% of public workers joined (IRIN 2005). The Netherlands gave $10 million to pay off retiring teachers so about 7,000 could be replaced (IMF letter).
card.confidence_note: Oxfam and teachers' unions blame IMF spending ceilings. The IMF says 'at no time' did its policies bar hiring teachers, and blames pay rises and unpaid retirement benefits.

sources.title: IMF preventing achievement of education MDG - Oxfam
The hard road to HIPC completion - Yearender
Letter by Thomas C. Dawson on Zambia (IMF External Relations)
Zambia: Letter of Intent, Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies
Press Release No. 05/79: IMF and World Bank support Zambia's completion point under HIPC

card.whole: The 2004 programme expected the wage bill to fall to 8% of GDP and the deficit to 4% of GDP, after a 6.6% deficit and 17.2% inflation in 2003 (IMF letter of intent). The IMF reported in April 2005 that the wage bill was held below 8% of GDP and that progress was made on inflation, and Zambia reached the HIPC completion point; the Times of Zambia reported that inflation fell below the programme target and that creditors had committed about US$3.8 billion of debt relief when Zambia reached the decision point in 2000. Oxfam said the wage cap left 12,000 trained teachers off the payroll while schools were short of about 9,000 (IRIN, undated report).
card.conditions: State employee wages were frozen for six months from February 2004; IRIN (2005) lists this among austerity measures prescribed by the international financial institutions, without naming it as a specific IMF or World Bank condition. Oxfam said IMF conditions capped public wages at 8% of GDP (IRIN 2004). The IMF says teachers, doctors and nurses were exempted from the hiring freeze in its November 2002 policy memorandum.
